title: DevOps & Deployment
blurb: How software is built, shipped and kept alive: servers, CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes, cloud, IaC and observability.

sections.title: Foundations
sections.blurb: The big picture: how code becomes a running product, environments, and why DevOps exists.

pages.title: The Big Picture: How Software Reaches Users
pages.summary: You wrote code on your laptop and it works. Between that and a stranger using it at 3 a.m. there is a long chain: build, package, ship, run, expose, monitor. DevOps is the discipline of making that chain fast, repeatable and safe.

pages.title: Environments: Dev, Staging, Production
pages.summary: An environment is a complete, isolated copy of "your system running somewhere": its own servers, database, config and secrets. Having more than one is how teams change software without gambling with real users.

pages.title: The Request Lifecycle
pages.summary: What really happens between typing a URL and seeing a page? Knowing every hop tells you where to look when something breaks, and which DevOps tool lives at which hop.

pages.title: DevOps Culture, History and Metrics
pages.summary: DevOps is first a way of working and only second a toolset. Understanding the problem it grew out of explains why every tool in this handbook looks the way it does.

pages.title: Glossary A to Z
pages.summary: Terms you will meet across this handbook, in plain language. Skim it now, return when a word trips you up.

sections.title: Linux & Servers
sections.blurb: What a server really is: shell, filesystem, permissions, processes, systemd, SSH.

pages.title: What Is a Server?
pages.summary: A server is just a computer that runs a program waiting for requests, usually with no screen or keyboard, always on, reachable over a network. There is no magic: everything you do on a server is something you can do on a Linux laptop.

pages.title: Shell Essentials
pages.summary: On a server there is usually no GUI. The shell is how you inspect, change and automate everything. A small set of commands and the idea of pipes cover 90% of daily work.

pages.title: Filesystem and Permissions
pages.summary: Linux treats almost everything as a file and controls access with a simple owner/group/other permission model. Most "permission denied" errors, and a large share of security incidents, trace back to this lesson.

pages.title: Processes and systemd
pages.summary: Your app on a server is a process. Production means that process starts at boot, restarts on crash, runs as the right user, has its logs captured and can be stopped cleanly. On modern Linux, systemd does all of that.

pages.title: SSH: Secure Remote Access
pages.summary: SSH is the front door to every server you will ever manage, and also what CI systems use to deploy. Understanding keys, the client config file, tunnels and hardening will save you hours and protect you from the most common attacks.

pages.title: Package Management and Runtimes
pages.summary: Installing software on a server should be repeatable, verifiable and updatable. Package managers give you that; downloading random tarballs and running "make install" gives you a snowflake.

pages.title: Logs and Troubleshooting
pages.summary: Something is broken at 2 a.m. The difference between a 5-minute fix and a 3-hour guessing game is knowing where logs live, which four resources can run out, and following a method rather than a hunch.

pages.title: Shell Scripting for Automation
pages.summary: A script is a saved list of commands that runs the same way every time. It is the first step from "I deployed it by hand" to "anyone (or any pipeline) can deploy it". The risk is that bash fails silently by default, so safe habits matter.

pages.title: Cron and Scheduled Automation
pages.summary: Backups, certificate renewals, log cleanup, report generation: servers constantly need things done on a schedule. Linux offers two tools, the classic cron and the modern systemd timers. Both fail quietly unless you design for it.

sections.title: Networking & the Web
sections.blurb: IPs, ports, DNS, HTTP, TLS, reverse proxies, load balancers, CDNs.

pages.title: IP Addresses, Ports and Sockets
pages.summary: Every deployment problem eventually becomes "can machine A reach machine B on port N?" This lesson gives you the mental model and the commands to answer that question in seconds instead of hours.

pages.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
pages.summary: Humans use names like app.example.com ; networks use IP addresses. DNS translates between them. It is also the root cause of a startling share of outages, and the lever you pull for most deployment cutovers.

pages.title: HTTP and HTTPS
pages.summary: HTTP is the language your app, browser, reverse proxy, load balancer and CDN all speak. Knowing it well turns mysterious 502s, stale caches and CORS errors into five-minute fixes.

pages.title: TLS and Certificates
pages.summary: TLS is what makes the padlock appear. Operationally it is about one thing: getting a valid certificate onto your server and renewing it before it expires. Expired certificates are among the most common, most embarrassing and most preventable outages.

pages.title: Reverse Proxies and nginx
pages.summary: A reverse proxy sits in front of your application and handles the messy edge of the internet: TLS, compression, static files, slow clients, rate limits. It is the first piece of infrastructure almost every production app gets, and nginx is the most common choice.

pages.title: Load Balancers
pages.summary: One server is a single point of failure and a scaling ceiling. A load balancer spreads traffic over many servers, removes unhealthy ones automatically, and lets you deploy without downtime.

pages.title: Firewalls and Security Groups
pages.summary: The moment a server gets a public IP, automated scanners find it, usually within minutes. A firewall decides which network traffic is allowed in and out. The guiding principle is simple: expose only what must be exposed.

pages.title: CDNs and Caching
pages.summary: Physics sets a floor on latency: a round trip from Sydney to a server in Virginia costs roughly 200 ms, however fast your code is. A CDN puts copies of your content near users and absorbs traffic before it ever reaches your servers.

sections.title: Deploying to a Server
sections.blurb: Ship an app by hand to a VPS, then learn strategies: blue-green, canary, rollbacks.

pages.title: Static vs Dynamic Hosting: What Goes Where
pages.summary: Before choosing tools, decide what kind of thing you are deploying. A pile of HTML and JavaScript files and a long-running server process have very different needs, costs and failure modes. Picking the simplest hosting that fits is the cheapest optimisation in DevOps.

pages.title: Manual Deploy to a VPS: Node.js, Postgres, nginx, HTTPS
pages.summary: This is the capstone of the first half of the handbook: take an Express app with a Postgres database from your laptop to a real domain over HTTPS on an Ubuntu server, by hand. Everything later (CI/CD, Docker, Terraform) automates exactly these steps, so doing them manually once is how you understand what the automation is doing.

pages.title: Process Managers: systemd, PM2, supervisor
pages.summary: Running node server.js in an SSH session works until you close the terminal, the process crashes, or the server reboots. A process manager keeps your app alive, restarts it when it fails, captures its logs and starts it at boot.

pages.title: Config and Secrets Basics
pages.summary: The same code must run on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production, talking to different databases with different credentials. The way to achieve this is to keep configuration out of the code. Secrets deserve extra care, because a leaked key is an incident, not a bug.

pages.title: Database Migrations in Deployments
pages.summary: Code is easy to roll back; data is not. The database schema is the one part of a deployment that carries state, and most "bad deploy" horror stories (locked tables, dropped columns, hours of downtime) are migration mistakes. Learn to change schemas safely while the app keeps running.

pages.title: Deployment Strategies
pages.summary: "Stop the old version, start the new one" works until the first time it fails with real users watching. Deployment strategies are different answers to one question: how do you move users from version A to version B while limiting the damage if B is broken?

pages.title: Zero-Downtime Deploys and Rollbacks
pages.summary: Users should never notice you deployed, and when a release is bad, you should be able to undo it in seconds, not hours. Both goals come from the same few techniques: graceful shutdown, health checks, atomic switching of releases, and a rehearsed rollback plan.

pages.title: The Deploy Checklist
pages.summary: Experienced engineers are not people who never break production; they are people who run the same boring checks every time. A checklist moves deployment from heroics to routine. Use this one as a starting point and edit it after every incident.

sections.title: Git & CI/CD
sections.blurb: Why pipelines matter, and how to build them with GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Jenkins.

pages.title: Why CI/CD Matters
pages.summary: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery are not "nice automation". They are the difference between a team that ships a change in an hour with confidence and a team that ships once a quarter with a prayer. This lesson explains the pain CI/CD removes, what it is worth in money and sleep, and how the industry measures it.

pages.title: Git Workflows: Branching, Reviews and Releases
pages.summary: CI/CD is only as good as the workflow that feeds it. How your team branches, reviews, merges and tags code determines how often you integrate, how risky releases are, and how easily you can trace what is running in production.

pages.title: Continuous Integration
pages.summary: Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared mainline frequently, and verifying each merge with an automated build and test run. It is a behavior first and a tool second.

pages.title: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
pages.summary: "CD" means two different things, and mixing them up causes real confusion. Both extend CI by automating the path to production. They differ in one decision: does a human press the final button?

pages.title: Anatomy of a Pipeline
pages.summary: Every CI/CD tool has its own syntax, but they all model the same thing: a graph of stages made of jobs made of steps, passing artifacts along, running on machines called runners. Learn the shape once and you can read any pipeline.

pages.title: GitHub Actions
pages.summary: GitHub Actions is the CI/CD system built into GitHub. Workflows are YAML files in your repo, triggered by repository events, executed on hosted or self-hosted runners. It is the most widely used CI system today; this lesson goes from concepts to a complete Node app pipeline that tests, builds and pushes a Docker image, and deploys over SSH.

pages.title: GitLab CI/CD
pages.summary: GitLab bundles source hosting, CI/CD, a container registry, security scanning and environments into one product. Its pipeline model, stages containing jobs, defined in a single .gitlab-ci.yml , is concise and has influenced many other tools.

pages.title: Jenkins and Other CI/CD Tools
pages.summary: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are not the only options. Jenkins is the veteran you will meet in many companies; CircleCI, Argo and Tekton cover other niches. This lesson shows what each is, how its pipeline looks, and how to choose.

pages.title: Secrets in Pipelines
pages.summary: A CI/CD pipeline is the most privileged automation in your company: it can read your source, publish to your registry and deploy to production. That makes it one of the most attractive targets for attackers. This lesson covers how to give pipelines the access they need, and nothing more.

pages.title: Testing and Quality Gates
pages.summary: A pipeline is only as trustworthy as the checks in it. A quality gate is an automated decision: "this change may proceed, or it may not". This lesson covers which checks to run, what each is good for, and how to turn them into gates that protect production without strangling developers.

pages.title: Pipeline Best Practices and Anti-Patterns
pages.summary: Building a first pipeline is easy. Keeping it fast, trusted and maintainable for years, with dozens of engineers and hundreds of repos, is the real craft. This lesson collects the practices that separate pipelines people love from pipelines people route around.

sections.title: Containers & Docker
sections.blurb: Images, layers, Dockerfiles, volumes, networks and Compose.

pages.title: Why Containers?
pages.summary: Containers exist to solve one stubborn problem: software that behaves differently depending on where it runs. A container packages your application together with everything it needs, then runs it as an isolated process on a shared kernel. It is not magic and it is not a tiny virtual machine, and once you see what it really is, most of Docker stops being mysterious.

pages.title: Docker Architecture and Installation
pages.summary: "Docker" is really a stack of cooperating pieces: a CLI, a daemon, a high-level runtime (containerd), a low-level runtime (runc), and open standards that tie them together. Knowing which piece does what makes error messages, alternatives like Podman, and Kubernetes' move away from Docker all make sense.

pages.title: Images and Layers
pages.summary: An image is not one big file. It is an ordered stack of immutable, content-addressed layers plus a small piece of JSON metadata. Understanding layers explains why builds are sometimes instant and sometimes slow, why pulls reuse downloads, why deleting a file in a later step does not shrink your image, and why tags are not the same as versions.

pages.title: Writing Dockerfiles
pages.summary: A Dockerfile is a text recipe: start from a base image, then run a series of instructions, each producing a layer. Writing a good one is mostly about knowing what each instruction really does, ordering them for the build cache, and keeping the result small, secure and well-behaved at shutdown.

pages.title: Multi-Stage Builds and Optimization
pages.summary: Compilers, dev dependencies and build tools are needed to build your app but are dead weight (and attack surface) when you run it. Multi-stage builds let one Dockerfile use a fat image to build and a tiny image to ship. Combine that with smart cache ordering, BuildKit features and multi-arch builds, and you get fast builds and small, safe images.

pages.title: Volumes and Data Persistence
pages.summary: A container's writable layer is born with the container and dies with it. Delete the container and every file it wrote is gone. That is perfect for stateless web apps and disastrous for databases. Volumes and mounts are how you attach durable storage to disposable containers.

pages.title: Docker Networking
pages.summary: Every container gets its own network namespace: its own IP address, interfaces and ports. Docker's job is to wire those namespaces together and to the outside world. Most "my containers cannot talk to each other" problems come down to five ideas: network drivers, user-defined networks with built-in DNS, port publishing, localhost meaning something different inside a container, and bind addresses.

pages.title: Docker Compose
pages.summary: Real applications are several containers: an API, a database, a cache, a reverse proxy. Starting each with a long docker run line, creating networks and volumes by hand and remembering the order is error-prone. Compose lets you describe the whole stack in one YAML file and manage it with a single command.

pages.title: Container Registries
pages.summary: An image on your laptop helps nobody else. A registry is the server that stores and distributes images, the "package repository" of the container world. Your CI pushes to it; your servers, Kubernetes clusters and teammates pull from it. How you tag, secure and scan what lives there decides how safe and repeatable your deployments are.

pages.title: Container Security and Best Practices
pages.summary: Containers share the host kernel, so their isolation is thinner than a VM's, and default settings are permissive. Security here is mostly about shrinking what a compromised process can do: run as an unprivileged user, drop capabilities, make the filesystem read-only, cap resources, keep secrets out of images and keep the contents patched.

pages.title: Debugging Containers
pages.summary: Containers fail in a small number of recurring ways: the process exits, gets killed, cannot reach something, or runs but behaves differently than on your laptop. A systematic routine, check the state, read the logs, inspect the config, get inside, compare environments, resolves most problems in minutes.

sections.title: Kubernetes
sections.blurb: Orchestration: pods, deployments, services, ingress, scaling, Helm.

pages.title: Why Container Orchestration?
pages.summary: Running one container on one server is easy. Running two hundred containers across thirty servers, keeping them healthy, updating them without downtime and scaling them with traffic is a different problem entirely. Orchestration is the software that solves it, and Kubernetes is the one that won.

pages.title: Kubernetes Architecture
pages.summary: A Kubernetes cluster is a set of machines split into a control plane that makes decisions and worker nodes that run your containers. Underneath, everything is one idea repeated many times: a controller compares desired state with actual state and closes the gap.

pages.title: Local Setup and kubectl Essentials
pages.summary: You do not need a cloud account to learn Kubernetes. A full cluster runs on your laptop in under a minute. This lesson sets one up, teaches the kubectl commands you will use daily, and dissects the shape of every Kubernetes YAML file.

pages.title: Pods and Workload Controllers
pages.summary: The Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit, but you almost never create one directly. You create a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) that manages Pods for you. Choosing the right controller is the core design decision for every workload.

pages.title: Services and Networking
pages.summary: Pods come and go and their IPs change constantly. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable name and virtual IP, and load-balances across the healthy ones. This lesson covers the Service types, cluster DNS, what kube-proxy really does, and how NetworkPolicy locks traffic down.

pages.title: Ingress and the Gateway API
pages.summary: Services expose ports; Ingress and Gateway expose HTTP(S) applications. They give you host and path routing, TLS termination and one shared entry point for dozens of services instead of one costly load balancer each.

pages.title: Configuration and Secrets
pages.summary: Build one image, run it everywhere. Anything that differs between environments (URLs, feature flags, passwords) is injected at runtime through ConfigMaps and Secrets. Handling this well, especially secrets, is where many clusters quietly go wrong.

pages.title: Storage: Volumes, PVs and PVCs
pages.summary: Container filesystems vanish when a container restarts. Anything that must survive, such as a database, uploaded files or a queue, needs a volume whose lifecycle is independent of the Pod. Kubernetes abstracts storage so your YAML does not care whether the disk is an EBS volume, a Google Persistent Disk or an NFS share.

pages.title: Probes, Resources and Autoscaling
pages.summary: Kubernetes can only keep your app healthy and right-sized if you tell it what healthy means and how much it needs. Probes, resource requests and limits, and autoscalers are the three levers that turn a pile of Pods into a resilient, efficient system.

pages.title: Rolling Updates and Rollbacks
pages.summary: Shipping a new version should not mean downtime. Kubernetes Deployments replace Pods gradually, only advancing when the new ones are healthy, and keep history so you can undo a bad release with one command.

pages.title: Helm and Kustomize
pages.summary: A real application is a dozen YAML files, and you need several copies of them: dev, staging, production, each slightly different. Copy-pasting YAML does not scale. Helm and Kustomize are the two standard answers: one templates, the other patches.

pages.title: Namespaces, RBAC and Pod Security
pages.summary: A cluster is shared by many teams, apps and automation. Without boundaries, one team's mistake deletes another's database. Namespaces partition the cluster, RBAC decides who can do what, quotas stop noisy neighbours, and Pod security keeps containers from escaping.

pages.title: Debugging Kubernetes
pages.summary: Things will go wrong: Pods that will not start, Services that return nothing, rollouts that hang. Debugging Kubernetes is a learnable skill built on a small toolkit and a consistent flow: read the status, read the events, read the logs, and narrow down.

pages.title: Managed Kubernetes and Alternatives
pages.summary: Running the Kubernetes control plane yourself (etcd backups, certificate rotation, upgrades) is a job. Almost everyone should let a cloud provider do it. This lesson compares EKS, GKE and AKS, covers lightweight distributions, explains where the money goes, and lists genuine alternatives.

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code
sections.blurb: Terraform, Ansible, immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

pages.title: Why Infrastructure as Code?
pages.summary: Servers, networks, databases and DNS records are infrastructure. If you create them by clicking through a cloud console, nobody can review, repeat or undo what you did. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means describing infrastructure in text files and letting a tool make reality match.

pages.title: Terraform Fundamentals
pages.summary: Terraform is the most widely used provisioning tool. You describe cloud resources in HCL, run terraform plan to preview exactly what will change, and terraform apply to make it so. This lesson builds a real example: a VM with a security group on AWS.

pages.title: Terraform State, Modules and Environments
pages.summary: State is Terraform's memory: the map between your code and real cloud resources. Understanding it, storing it safely, splitting code into reusable modules and organising environments are what separate a demo from a team-ready setup.

pages.title: Terraform in CI/CD
pages.summary: Running terraform apply from a laptop works until two people do it at once, someone applies uncommitted code, or the person with production credentials is on holiday. Moving Terraform into a pipeline makes infrastructure changes reviewed, auditable and consistent, using the same pull-request workflow as application code.

pages.title: Ansible and Configuration Management
pages.summary: Terraform creates the server; something must then install packages, write config files and start services. Configuration management tools do this declaratively and repeatably across many machines. Ansible is the most popular because it needs nothing installed on the targets except SSH and Python.

pages.title: Immutable Infrastructure and Golden Images
pages.summary: Instead of logging into servers to patch and tweak them, build a fresh, fully configured image, deploy it, and throw the old servers away. Immutable infrastructure eliminates drift by never modifying a running machine. Packer is the tool that builds the images.

pages.title: GitOps
pages.summary: GitOps takes infrastructure as code one step further: git is the single source of truth for what should run, and an automated agent inside the environment continuously makes reality match it. Deployments become pull requests; rollbacks become reverts.

sections.title: Cloud Platforms
sections.blurb: IaaS/PaaS/serverless, AWS core services, scaling and high availability.

pages.title: What Is "The Cloud"?
pages.summary: "The cloud" is just other people's computers, rented by the second, controlled by an API. That sounds trivial, but the API part changes everything: infrastructure becomes something you can create, change and destroy from code, in minutes, without buying hardware or filing a ticket.

pages.title: AWS Core Services: The Essential Map
pages.summary: AWS has 200+ services, but a typical production web application uses about a dozen. Learn these well and you can read almost any architecture diagram. The same concepts exist on Google Cloud and Azure under different names.

pages.title: VPC and Cloud Networking
pages.summary: A Virtual Private Cloud is your own isolated slice of the provider's network. You decide the IP ranges, which machines face the internet, and which are hidden. Getting this layer right is the single biggest security and reliability decision in your cloud design.

pages.title: IAM and Access Control
pages.summary: Identity and Access Management answers one question for every API call: who is asking, and are they allowed to do this to that ? Most cloud security incidents are IAM failures, so this is the most valuable cloud skill to get right.

pages.title: Compute Options: VMs, Containers, Kubernetes, Serverless
pages.summary: "Where does my code run?" has five serious answers in the cloud. Each trades control for convenience. Choosing well is mostly about your team's size, your traffic shape, and how much operations work you are willing to own.

pages.title: PaaS and Modern Platforms
pages.summary: Platform-as-a-Service products let you git push and get a running, HTTPS-enabled, autoscaled application. They bundle what the earlier lessons made you assemble by hand: networking, load balancing, certificates, deploys, logs. For many products, this is the right answer for years.

pages.title: Databases and Storage in the Cloud
pages.summary: Compute is disposable; data is not. State is where cloud projects get hurt: lost backups, corrupt failovers, surprise bills. This lesson covers the three kinds of storage, managed databases, backups, replicas and the S3 patterns you will use constantly.

pages.title: Scaling and High Availability
pages.summary: Two questions drive production architecture. Scaling : can the system handle more load? High availability (HA) : does it keep working when parts fail? Hardware fails, deploys break, traffic spikes. The cloud gives you the tools; design is up to you.

pages.title: Cost Management and FinOps
pages.summary: In the data center, you spent money when you bought hardware. In the cloud, every engineer's API call can spend money, continuously. Without discipline, bills grow faster than revenue. FinOps is the practice of making cost visible, owned and optimised, by engineers as well as finance.

sections.title: Monitoring & Reliability
sections.blurb: Logs, metrics, traces, alerting, SLOs, incidents and postmortems.

pages.title: Why Observability?
pages.summary: Deploying is half the job. The other half is knowing, at any moment, whether your system is working for users and, when it isn't, finding out why in minutes rather than hours. Production is where software meets reality, and reality is full of surprises that no test suite predicted.

pages.title: Logging
pages.summary: Logs are the oldest telemetry: a diary your program writes about what it is doing. Done well they let you reconstruct any request after the fact. Done badly they are an expensive pile of unsearchable text, or worse, a leak of customer secrets.

pages.title: Metrics and Prometheus
pages.summary: Metrics are numbers sampled over time: requests per second, error ratio, memory in use, queue depth. They are tiny and cheap to store, which makes them the best signal for dashboards and alerts. Prometheus is the de facto open-source system for collecting and querying them.

pages.title: Distributed Tracing
pages.summary: In a microservice system one user click may touch ten services. Metrics tell you the checkout is slow; logs from ten services are a haystack. A trace shows the whole journey of one request as a timeline, revealing exactly which hop spent the time or failed.

pages.title: Alerting
pages.summary: An alert is a machine tapping a human on the shoulder: "come look at this now". Every alert spends a scarce resource, human attention, and often sleep. Good alerting wakes people only for problems that matter and that they can act on. Bad alerting trains them to ignore the pager.

pages.title: SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets
pages.summary: "The site should be fast and reliable" is not an engineering target. SRE replaces vague goals with numbers: measure what users experience (SLI), decide how good is good enough (SLO), and treat the gap to perfection as a budget you can spend on shipping features.

pages.title: Incident Response and Postmortems
pages.summary: Outages are inevitable. What distinguishes mature teams is not that they never have incidents, but that they respond in a calm, coordinated way, restore service fast, and learn so the same failure does not recur. This lesson is the playbook.

pages.title: Health Checks and Uptime Monitoring
pages.summary: Before anything else can work (load balancing, autoscaling, rolling deploys, alerting) the platform needs a cheap way to ask your service: "are you OK?" Health checks are that question. Synthetic monitoring and status pages extend it to "does it work from the user's side, and do users know?"

pages.title: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Patterns
pages.summary: In distributed systems, partial failure is the normal state. Networks drop packets, dependencies slow down, instances disappear. Resilient software expects this and degrades gracefully. Chaos engineering goes further: it breaks things on purpose, in a controlled way, to prove the resilience is real.

sections.title: Production Readiness
sections.blurb: Security, secrets, backups, databases, scaling patterns, the 12-factor app.

pages.title: The Twelve-Factor App
pages.summary: The twelve-factor methodology (written by Heroku engineers around 2011) is still the best short checklist for building applications that are easy to deploy, scale and operate. Almost every modern platform, from Docker to Kubernetes, assumes your app follows it.

pages.title: Secrets Management
pages.summary: Passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys and certificates are the keys to your kingdom. Most real-world breaches involve a leaked credential rather than a clever exploit. This lesson covers where secrets should live, how to hand them to applications, how to rotate them and what to do the minute one leaks.

pages.title: Server and Application Hardening
pages.summary: A public server is probed within minutes of getting an IP address. Hardening is the unglamorous work of shrinking what an attacker can reach and limiting what they can do if they get in. Most of it is a one-time checklist plus automation.

pages.title: DevSecOps and Supply Chain Security
pages.summary: Your application is perhaps 10% code you wrote and 90% code you imported, plus a base image, a build system and a pipeline. Attackers know it: compromising one popular package or one CI token reaches thousands of victims. DevSecOps means building security checks into the pipeline so they run on every change, not once a year.

pages.title: Databases in Production
pages.summary: Your stateless app servers are cattle; the database is the one pet you cannot lose. It is usually the first bottleneck, the hardest thing to scale and the source of the worst outages. This lesson covers connection management, replicas, indexes, safe migrations, the managed-vs-self-hosted decision and caching, with Postgres as the running example.

pages.title: Backups and Disaster Recovery
pages.summary: Nobody wants a backup; everybody wants a restore. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. This lesson covers what to protect, how often, how to store it safely, and how to choose a disaster recovery strategy that matches your budget and tolerance for downtime.

pages.title: Scaling Patterns
pages.summary: Scaling means keeping latency and error rates acceptable as load grows. There is no single trick; there is a toolbox, and a rule: measure first, then apply the cheapest pattern that removes the actual bottleneck. This lesson walks through the toolbox from cheap to expensive.

pages.title: Performance and Load Testing
pages.summary: You do not know how your system behaves under load until you load it. Load testing finds the breaking point before your customers do, and gives you the numbers needed for capacity planning. This lesson shows how to test with k6, how to read the results and how to hunt the bottleneck.

pages.title: Production Readiness Checklist
pages.summary: "Are we ready to go live?" is answered best with a checklist, not a feeling. Airline pilots use them because memory fails under pressure; so do mature engineering teams. Use this as a launch review: every row should be a tick, a conscious "not needed, because...", or a tracked ticket with an owner.

sections.title: Practice & Roadmap
sections.blurb: A capstone project, cheat sheets and a learning roadmap.

pages.title: Capstone Overview: Ship a Real Service End to End
pages.summary: Reading about DevOps does not make you a DevOps engineer; shipping does. In this capstone you will take a small API plus a Postgres database through every stage of the handbook: containerize it, build a CI pipeline, deploy to a real server with HTTPS, define the server with Terraform and watch it with Prometheus and Grafana.

pages.title: Capstone: Containerize the App
pages.summary: Stage 1: package Notely and its database so that docker compose up gives any teammate (or any server) an identical environment in one command. This is the "build once, run anywhere" step everything else depends on.

pages.title: Capstone: Build the CI Pipeline
pages.summary: Stage 2: every push to GitHub should automatically run the tests, build the Docker image and publish it to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) with an immutable tag. After this, "what is running in production" is answered by a commit SHA.

pages.title: Capstone: Deploy to a VPS
pages.summary: Stage 3: put Notely on a real server behind nginx with a Let's Encrypt certificate, and make the pipeline update it automatically with minimal downtime. This is the same flow as a "real" deployment, just without the orchestrator.

pages.title: Capstone: Infrastructure as Code and Monitoring
pages.summary: Stage 4: stop clicking in a provider dashboard. Describe the server, firewall and DNS record in Terraform so the whole environment can be rebuilt from git, then add Prometheus, Grafana and an external uptime check so you find out about problems before your users do.

pages.title: The Six-Month DevOps Learning Roadmap
pages.summary: DevOps is wide, and the most common mistake is learning tools in random order. This roadmap sequences topics so each month builds on the last, pairs every month with a concrete project and names the milestone that tells you you are done. It assumes roughly 8-10 hours a week and a working knowledge of programming.

pages.title: Cheat Sheets
pages.summary: Dense, scannable reference tables for the commands you will use daily. Bookmark this page; the goal is recall speed, not explanation. Each section links back to a lesson for the why.

pages.title: DevOps Interview Questions and Strong Answers
pages.summary: Forty realistic questions grouped by topic, each with a concise answer of the kind that impresses an interviewer. Do not memorise the wording: understand the reasoning, add an example from your own projects, and be ready for the follow-up "why?" and "what are the trade-offs?".
